newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl allies pressure German employers on jobs.
newsitem.headline: Kohl allies pressure German employers on jobs.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition government, looking increasingly unlikely to fulfil a pledge to halve unemployment by the turn of the century, is stepping up the pressure on employers to create new jobs.

With unemployment at post-unification highs and rising, Kohl and his ministers are putting the blame on company bosses for failing to hire workers despite cuts in employment costs pushed through parliament this autumn.

"I expect employers to roll up their sleeves and say 'Now we're going to create jobs'," Kohl told the weekend party congress of the Christian Social Union (CSU), 14-year coalition partners with his Christian Democrats (CDU).

Unemployment in October rose to a record high of 4.04 million, seasonally adjusted. Germany's leading institutes have said they expected the number to stay above four million in 1997 despite forecasting economic recovery.
Employer groups fired back that Bonn's efforts have barely dented the high costs of adding workers to payrolls in Germany's highly regulated social market economy.

"The policies of the past year have hardly helped us to improve out competitive position," Dieter Hundt, incoming president of the Federation of Employers Associations, told the Welt am Sonntag newspaper.

Bonn has lowered sick pay allowances from 100 percent of a worker's wage to 80 percent, and made it easier for small companies to lay off workers. But, in the face of stiff labour resistance, sick pay cuts have not yet been implemented.
Employers want Bonn to press ahead with cuts in corporate taxes and company contributions to social security and pensions. Pensions charges are due to rise on January 1.

Criticism of company bosses has been mounting from the Kohl coalition since his parliamentary lieutenant Wolfgang Schaeuble said last week they had "glaringly failed" to create new jobs despite the welfare cutbacks.
Also speaking at the weekend, CSU party chief and Finance Minister Theo Waigel appealed to "the patriotism of employers" and urged them to invest in Germany, not abroad.
Waigel also warned that high unemployment could leave employers with a leftist government of Social Democrats, Greens and former east German Communists after elections in 1998.
Noting that several German companies recently announced job cuts at the same time as profit increases, Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said firms have to do more than slash costs.
"It may be that the greatest cost-cutter with the most dismissals is not the best," Rexrodt, a member of the liberal Free Democrats, told Welt am Sonntag.

Labour Minister Norbert Bluem, who has reiterated the commitment to halve unemployment, criticised the "current corporate philosophy" of letting workers go to get a short-term boost on the stock market.

"Corporations have a responsibility," Friedhelm Ost, the coalition's chairman of the economic committee in the lower house of parliament, said. "They must create jobs. We will hold them to this duty."

Analysts said the war of words could mark the start of a serious confrontation, but even a clash between the government and employers would be better for bosses than the alternative at elections due in 1998.

"It's not a bad strategy for Kohl. If the unemployment situation doesn't get better, that could open to door for a red-green coalition, and corporations don't want that," Gernot Nerb, analyst at Salomon Brothers in Frankfurt, said. -- Bonn newsroom, 49-228-26097150
